HCI / Product Design • Human-AI Interaction • 2026

AI-Augmented Journaling: Usability-Driven Redesign

Usability TestingInteraction DesignHuman-AI InteractionResearch AnalysisIterative Redesign
78%faster selected-text prompting
88%faster emotion filtering
0filtering misclicks in Round 2
78 → 83SUS score improvement

Problem

The journaling system could detect emotions, generate reflective prompts, and show emotional trends, but users struggled to understand what the AI was using, how selected text changed the prompt context, and how filtering worked on the trends page.

My role

I worked across research, interaction design, validation, and implementation: planning two rounds of moderated testing with 10 participants, analyzing breakdowns, redesigning core interactions, and implementing validated changes in the product.

What the research revealed

Users could not always tell what context the AI was using, selected text did not provide enough visible feedback, and the trend filters behaved differently from the selection model people expected. Behavioral data also showed that one planned feature offered less value than the team had assumed.

What changed—and why

I made selected states more obvious, clarified the boundary between AI-generated and manual actions, simplified the action hierarchy, and changed the filtering logic to follow a “select first, then add” mental model. We also removed the low-engagement feature so the product could focus on the AI interactions users valued more.

Validation & implementation

The second round showed substantial improvements in speed, accuracy, and perceived usability. I then implemented the validated interaction changes using GitHub Copilot and OpenAI Codex, carrying the work from research evidence into a functional experience.

Takeaway

The biggest gains did not require changing the AI model. Clearer state, feedback, and user control were enough to make the system feel considerably more understandable and dependable.

AI Product • Chrome Extension • nwHacks 2026

Negotiagent: AI-Powered Marketplace Negotiation

ReactTypeScriptChrome ExtensionGemini APIPrompt EngineeringAI UX
  • Built during nwHacks: a working browser extension concept for sellers managing marketplace conversations.
  • Kept users in control: AI drafts could be reviewed, confirmed, or rewritten before sending.
  • Product focus: balanced automation with trust, context, and human agency.

Problem

Sellers on peer-to-peer marketplaces often answer repetitive negotiation messages, schedule pickups, and respond quickly while trying to avoid mistakes. Fully autonomous messaging can feel risky, but manual replies are time-consuming.

What I built

Negotiagent is a Chrome extension side panel that reads listing context, drafts negotiation responses using Gemini 2.0 Flash, and gives the seller a clear approve/rewrite workflow before anything is sent.

Product thinking

The key design choice was not “let AI take over,” but “let AI reduce friction while the user stays accountable.” This makes the product more realistic for high-trust communication and resale transactions.

Product / UX Design • Figma • 2025

Smart Wardrobe Application

FigmaUser ResearchUsability TestingPrototypingRecommendation UX
  • Designed core user flows: closet intake, outfit creation, saved outfits, laundry tracking, and recommendation-ready styling.
  • Validated product risk: users need confidence in the digitized closet before trusting automated outfit suggestions.
  • Compared input methods: photo capture, barcode scanning, and web search for wardrobe digitization.
Digitize clothing
Organize the closet
Build an outfit
Save or wear it
Track availability

Overview

I designed and tested a medium-to-high-fidelity wardrobe management prototype in Figma. The experience supports closet organization, outfit planning, laundry visibility, saved outfit history, and a foundation for future styling recommendations.

Research & validation

I conducted need-finding research around wardrobe organization and outfit selection, then tested the prototype to identify friction across multi-step flows. I also compared photo capture, barcode scanning, and web search as different ways to digitize clothing.

Three decisions that shaped the product

Digitization: offer more than one intake path because speed, accuracy, and available product data vary. Outfit canvas: keep composition flexible without making the screen feel like a blank design tool. Laundry state: make item availability visible so the product does not recommend clothes the user cannot wear.

Product insight

People were more open to intelligent outfit suggestions once they trusted the accuracy of the closet underneath them. That shifted the design priority from “show the smartest recommendation” to “first make the wardrobe complete, editable, and believable.”

Machine Learning • FinTech • 2025

Credit Card Default Prediction Model

Pythonscikit-learnXGBoostSHAPFeature EngineeringModel Evaluation
  • Modeled 30,000 records: built an end-to-end credit default risk pipeline using 24 features.
  • Final ROC-AUC: 0.776: XGBoost performed best after comparing multiple models.
  • Made predictions explainable: used SHAP and permutation importance to communicate risk drivers.

Problem

Credit default prediction is not only a technical classification task; it needs careful feature design, threshold interpretation, and explainability so model outputs can be understood in a financial context.

My role

I built the machine learning pipeline, engineered payment-ratio features, addressed class imbalance, compared Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost, and analyzed feature importance for business interpretation.

Why explainability mattered

A risk score is only useful if people can understand what is driving it and decide how to respond. My banking experience made that especially concrete: a technically stronger model is not automatically a better product if its reasoning cannot be communicated or responsibly used.

UX Research • Product Strategy • A/B Testing • 2026

Hobby Discovery System

Product DiscoveryA/B TestingUsability TestingFigmaQuant + Qual Analysis
  • Ran an 8-participant A/B study: compared whether committed hobbies were easier to find under Matches or Profile.
  • Found a clearer navigation pattern: Matches placement averaged 2.5 clicks and 0.5 error clicks, compared with 5.25 clicks and 2.5 error clicks under Profile.
  • Validated layered information design: users rated information sufficiency highly and responded well to seeing quick summaries first, then richer detail pages.
Discover a hobby
Review practical details
Match based on fit
Choose to commit
Find it in Matches

Problem

Young adults often want to try new hobbies but get stuck early because they are unsure about time commitment, cost, equipment, location, social format, and beginner-friendly entry points. Beyond matching users to hobbies, the product also needed to clarify the difference between being interested in a hobby and actually committing to pursue it.

My role

I led product and UX direction for our four-person team, helping define the MVP, experience requirements, research priorities, and project timeline. I also worked on the medium-fidelity Figma prototype, experiment design, participant sessions, observation notes, Qualtrics questionnaire, and analysis.

Experiment insight

All participants first navigated to Matches when looking for committed hobbies, which suggested that users mentally connect commitment with the matching flow more than with profile information. The results were directional rather than statistically conclusive because of the small sample, but the click and error-click patterns gave a clear design signal.

Post-study iteration

I revised the product direction so committed hobbies stay within Matches, with the difference between “this fits me” and “I’m ready to pursue this” made explicit through labeling and calls to action. The next card interaction also uses clearer tap controls instead of relying on a swipe gesture that most participants did not discover.

Takeaway

The study reminded me that information architecture is often visible in people’s first instinct. Every participant went to Matches first; the better product decision was to respect that mental model instead of asking users to learn the team’s original structure.

Autonomous Maze Navigation Robot

ArduinoSensor IntegrationBayesian ReasoningMotor ControlTeam Project

My role

What I learned

Java • GUI Development • Object-Oriented Design • 2024

LingoLeap: Multiplayer Word Game

JavaSwing GUIOOPUMLPersistence
  • Built multiplayer gameplay: supported 3+ players, categories, scoring, and input validation.
  • Designed maintainable architecture: separated UI, game logic, event logging, and JSON persistence.
  • Created extensible rules: structured scoring so categories and bonus/penalty logic could evolve.

Problem

The goal was to build a usable multiplayer word game while keeping the architecture clean enough to support persistence, event history, and future feature changes.

My role

I implemented the game logic, Java Swing interface, class structure, event log, and JSON read/write flow while using UML to reason about relationships between classes.

Architecture choices

I separated the interface, game rules, event history, and persistence so each part could change without forcing a rewrite of the others. UML helped me catch overly tangled relationships before they became harder to debug in code.

Experience
